title: Phase-Structured Transformer: Design Constraints and Implementation Pathways That a Temporal Organization Layer Imposes on Attention Architectures
content: The computation graph of the Transformer is structurally “timeless”: all tokens within a layer receive homogeneous compute, no cross-request internal state is retained after a forward pass, and parameter updates do not distinguish the time scales of online adaptation and offline consolidation. In addition, there are three structural gaps: content and resources are not separated, the forward pass retains no traceable state, and parameter updates lack temporal stratification. This paper translates five transferable kernels of the source framework (the overall framework of consciousness engineering described in Ref. [25] and Ref. [26], hereafter uniformly referred to as the source framework or the source literature)—three nested clocks, the micro-epoch record, phase and duty cycle, the orthogonal decomposition of content state and resource state, and the five design principles T1–T5—into five components of the Phase-Structured Transformer (PST): dual-phase attention, gain-modulated attention with content–resource decoupling, a micro-epoch-woven three-stage information flow (an eight-operator non-isomorphic pipeline), slow-clock validation gating with a shadow KV cache, and a tri-temporal rhythm embedding. The formal results show that standard multi-head attention is the identity-reduction special case of this framework when ω = 1, the gains are equal, τ = 1, and k = n; the duty cycle ω is simultaneously a cognitive parameter and a compute-budget parameter; and the phase-resolved evaluation protocol suggests that a number of earlier “no significant difference” conclusions may stem from cross-phase averaging. This paper provides unified formal definitions, a phase-resolved complexity table, a consolidated list of falsifiable hypotheses (M1–M14), and a minimal ablation matrix (A0–A9). This paper does not claim that Transformers are conscious, nor that biological constants (15 Hz, a gain ratio of 1.21, κ ≈ 0) should be literally copied as hyperparameters; its core claim can be compressed into one sentence: “balancing the global and the focal” need not be achieved by compromising on a single distribution, but can be achieved by focusing and covering at different moments while faithfully preserving what is suppressed—a claim that is testable and falsifiable.
